implementation_notes: Scala replaces the Policy object with a value - type Policy[R] = (SecurityContext, Action, R) => Decision - so rules are ordinary functions that compose; the guard is a higher-order method that evaluates the decision before running the operation, and pattern guards (case req if policy(req) =>) express the same check inside a match (docs.scala-lang.org: pattern guards). What replaces the classic structure: function values and partial functions replace the Policy/Guard classes, and a by-name parameter defers the resource operation until after the decision. The trait-based policy with identity and configuration is still justified when rules need shared state or a rule table loaded from configuration.
idiom_name: type Policy[R] = (SecurityContext, Action, R) => Decision + guard method
pitfalls: The operation must be a by-name (op: => T) or otherwise deferred parameter; a strict parameter runs the resource code before the decision.
Pattern-guard matches that fall through without a deny branch silently skip enforcement; always end with a catch-all that denies.
Function-valued policies compose easily but also bypass easily: keep the guarded entry point the only public API, not an unguarded low-level method.

variants.name: Scala 3 context parameters + Policy type class
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3 makes the security context an implicit dependency: the guarded operation takes op: SecurityContext ?=> T and the method asks for the policy and context with using clauses - or relies on a given Policy[R] instance - so the context is threaded by the compiler instead of through every signature (docs.scala-lang.org: contextual abstractions establish context and express capabilities). What replaces the classic structure: using clauses and given instances replace explicitly passed Policy/Guard objects, while the check remains an ordinary call before the deferred operation. Choose this when the context would otherwise appear in dozens of signatures; prefer explicit parameters when the codebase is read by non-Scala engineers or multiple contexts coexist.
variants.code_sketch:
def guarded[R, T](a: Action, r: R)(op: SecurityContext ?=> T)
                 (using ctx: SecurityContext, p: Policy[R]): T =
  p.decide(ctx, a, r) match
    case Left(reason) => throw AccessDenied(reason)
    case Right(_)     => op(using ctx)
pitfalls: Implicit resolution picks a given by type: two SecurityContext instances in scope make the decision depend on the import site; keep exactly one canonical instance and no anonymous fallback.
A default or global given context would silently substitute an unauthenticated subject - never provide one.
Context functions (SecurityContext ?=> T) hide the dependency from readers and refactoring tools; document the guard contract where the operation is defined, not only where it is called.
